Hi everyone,

I'd like to share some progress towards the formalization of CFSG (github). Currently we have formalized the following

  • the odd order theorem (following Bender-Glauberman and Peterfalvi)
  • the classification of groups with strongly embedded subgroups (GLS4, theorem SE/Bender-Suzuki)
  • the classification of groups with quaternion/dihedral Sylow 2-subgroups
  • basic properties of some sporadic groups, including Mathieu groups, HS, J2, McL, Fischer groups (following ATLAS; will be released soon)
  • some basic properties of K-groups (GLS3; will be released soon)

The repo also contains comparator setup for the Bender-Suzuki theorem and the solvable case of Glauberman's ZJ theorem.
What's your estimate on how close to complete lean proof of CFSG this is (assuming some favorable conditions like no major errors found that need to be fixed, etc)?

It's still quite far, but I think it can be completed in few years, given sufficient resource. Most of the arguments (in GLS series) rely on defining K-groups upfront (which means each sporadic group needs to be defined and properties of these sporadic group proven). However, it's still a huge pain the construct these groups and formalize ATLAS, even with the help of AI.
That's amazing. Is Thompson's N groups paper on your todo list? I think of that as being sort of like a sequel to the odd order theorem.

Tianjiao Nie said:

It's still quite far, but I think it can be completed in few years, given sufficient resource.

Are you assuming that the GLS series itself will be completed by then? I'm hoping that will be true, but maybe you're guessing that even if the official GLS project isn't quite done, AI will be able to fill in the rest?

Tau Ceti has a statement ready now, see #Project announcements > Statement of the classification of finite simple groups @ 💬

I only noticed this discussion after posting my announcement. In particular, I had not seen Tianjiao's comment that constructing the groups and formalizing the ATLAS is one of the major bottlenecks for the CFSG project.

So the two developments were genuinely independent, but they appear to fit together rather naturally. I would be very interested in comparing the constructions and seeing what can be shared between the projects.

I would like to comment on the statement of the classification of finite simple groups. In a certain sense, I have been trying to understand it for more than thirty years, and there are still aspects that I find difficult to pin down. I am not a finite-group theorist, so some of these difficulties may simply reflect my unfamiliarity with the literature.

First, there is a numerical formulation that does not require choosing explicit constructions:

"Take the usual arithmetic list of finite-simple-group orders, supplemented by explicitly specified, isomorphism-invariant information distinguishing the known equal-order cases. Every finite simple group has one of these refined numerical types, and each type is realized by exactly one finite simple group up to isomorphism."

Here one must distinguish exceptional isomorphisms, which give different names for the same group, from genuine order collisions between nonisomorphic groups. The latter consist of the B_n(q), C_n(q) pairs for odd q and n >= 3, and the pair Alt_8, PSL_3(4). At those orders, the extra information distinguishes two possibilities.

This is one formulation that I would like to see formalized and ultimately proved. Once the arithmetic list and the discriminators have been specified, writing down the statement should be straightforward. Of course, this says nothing about the difficulty of proving it.

A second formulation is that every finite simple group is isomorphic to one of a specified collection of explicitly constructed groups. As I understand it, this is the approach taken in the Tau Ceti development. This provides more concrete mathematical objects, but defining a model is only the beginning: one must prove that it has the expected order and is simple. In some cases, these are substantial mathematical problems in their own right, quite apart from their formalization.

I have little to add concerning the cyclic, alternating, and Lie-type groups. Their constructions are comparatively familiar. There is a minor organizational question about where to place the Tits group, but this does not affect the substance of the classification.

For the sporadic groups, my own preference is to characterize them through independently meaningful mathematical objects. For example, M_24 is the automorphism group of the extremal doubly-even self-dual binary code of length 24, the Golay code. Similarly, 2.Co_1 = Co_0 is the automorphism group of the extremal positive-definite even unimodular lattice of rank 24, the Leech lattice. These descriptions connect the groups with objects characterized by simple intrinsic conditions.

The analogous description for the Monster would use the extremal self-dual (also called holomorphic) vertex operator algebra of central charge 24. Here, however, the uniqueness assertion remains conjectural: the Moonshine module V^\natural is conjectured to be the unique strongly rational self-dual VOA of central charge 24 with V_1 = 0. This should be distinguished from the established identification of the automorphism group of the explicitly constructed Moonshine module.

One can therefore follow one of the viewpoints in Richard Borcherds' article "What is the Monster?" and simply define the Monster as Aut(V^\natural). The substantial task is then to derive its group-theoretic properties from that definition.

For me, tracing the precise literature connecting this definition with the order and the group-theoretic characterizations of the Monster has been difficult. When following references, I have repeatedly encountered citations to unpublished results or statements whose published proofs I could not locate. This is not a claim that the necessary proofs are unavailable; it is a description of the difficulty an outsider can have in reconstructing the dependency chain.

My joint work with Martin Seysen addresses part of this problem. We give a self-contained, computer-assisted computation of the order of an explicitly generated group acting on the Griess algebra. We then identify it with the full automorphism group of the Griess algebra and of V^\natural, using Borcherds' proof of Monstrous Moonshine and results of Scott Carnahan. These are separate steps, with different inputs.

The twenty sporadic groups in the "happy family" occur as subquotients of the Monster, including the Monster itself. Nevertheless, it remains useful to find, for an individual group, a natural object X whose automorphism group is that group, rather than merely locating it inside a larger group.

For example, I would like a characterization of M_11 to start from the ternary Golay code, with the relevant automorphism convention made explicit. I would then like to understand directly how this accounts for its appearance as the automorphism group of the Adler curve: the ordinary genus-26 curve X(11) over the algebraic closure of F_3. The treatments I have encountered seem to use some classification input at the identification stage.

For the Fischer groups, the Conway-Parker algebra provides a natural starting point; its relationship with V^\natural is part of ongoing work. I hope that comparable descriptions can be developed for the other members of the happy family.

That leaves the six pariahs. I now have a much clearer understanding of the Rudvalis group, and also the Tits group, through the Conway-Wales lattice. For J_3, O'Nan, and J_1, I would like similarly transparent lattice-based descriptions. For the Lyons group and J_4, the realizations I know do not yet give me the same conceptual understanding. This is a statement about what I find mathematically explanatory, not an objection to the validity of those constructions.

Returning to formalization, the connection between the models in my constructive ATLAS and the recognition theorems used in a proof of CFSG is not always clear to me. Proving order and simplicity establishes an existence result. Without invoking classification, it does not automatically supply every structural property needed by a particular recognition argument.

For Fi_22 and Fi_23, I have been able to make this connection using Aschbacher's book on the Fischer groups. For Fi_24', the route through that book imports further results from his treatment of the Monster. I would need to identify precisely which statements are required and then establish them in my model. For Rudvalis, I do not yet know which characterization the intended CFSG development will use, but I expect that the required properties could be proved and formalized directly from the lattice construction once they are specified.

So my practical question is: what precise recognition statements should a library of explicitly constructed finite simple groups provide to a CFSG formalization? The numerical formulation gives a compact final statement. The constructive formulation gives concrete models. Connecting those models to the hypotheses and conclusions of the chosen classification proof seems to be a separate task that would benefit from being made explicit.

@Gerald Hoehn, I like how you are presenting sporadic groups using symmetries of exceptional objects rather than using the explicit presentations that we see in Tau Ceti. These objects are interesting in their own right, and it would be great to have a collection of formalized constructions of such exceptional objects together with proofs of useful properties.
At the moment, linear codes in Mathlib are in development in #38014 but progress appears to have stalled in the past few months.
I would guess that the CFSG formalization will follow the GLS approach pretty closely. GLS relies on Aschbacher and Smith, so I would guess that that's how the Rudvalis group fits in?

@Timothy Chow The AI tells me that Aschbacher and Smith need for the identification of Rudvalis two properties: (Ru1) and (Ru2). Both can be seen in my construction. (Ru1) seems obvious and (Ru2) needs some computation, so it may be slightly harder to formalize. If someone comes up with explicit (Ru1) and (Ru2) formalizations, it seems not be too hard to show that my Atlas Rudvalis satisfies it.

Ryan Smith said:

That's amazing. Is Thompson's N groups paper on your todo list? I think of that as being sort of like a sequel to the odd order theorem.

@Ryan Smith We've finished the formalization of the classification of N_2-groups (and thus the classification of minimal finite simple groups). The raw code is available at https://github.com/Qiuzhen-CFSG/CFSG/tree/sync-1003 . We're still trying to clean up a little bit.
